Stack Exchange network consists of 183 Q&A communities including Stack Overflow, the largest, most trusted online community for developers to learn, share their knowledge, and build their careers. ### current community. ### your communities. ### more stack exchange communities. # Sensitivity of KL Divergence. I am very new to the concept of KL divergence. Although I have grasped the fundamental formulations, I have a confusion comparing the KL divergence across the different distributions. How do I determine the best distribution that matches the distribution of $\textbf{x}$? I understand the lower the KL divergence, the better matching, but what would be the sensitivity of the KL divergence parameter, following which we can say that the distribution is significantly different? ## 1 Answer 1. How do I determine the best distribution that matches the distribution of $\textbf{x}$?". is much more general than the scope of the KL-divergence (also known as relative entropy). And if a goodness-of-fit like result is desired, it might be better to first take a look at tests such as the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Shapiro-Wilk, or Cramer-von-Mises test. I believe those tests are much more common for questions of goodness-of-fit than anything involving the KL-divergence. The KL-divergence is more commonly used as a measure of information gain, when going from a prior distribution to a posterior distribution in Monte Carlo simulations. All that said, here we go with my actual answer:. Note that the Kullback-Leibler divergence from $q$ to $p$, defined through. D\_{KL}(p|q) = \int p \log\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) dx. It does satisfy positivity $D\_{KL}(p|q)\ge0$, though, with equality holding if and only if $p=q$. This is used e.g. in `R`'s package `vsgoftest` implementing the Vasicek-Song test, which will provide you with a p-value where you can use the commonly used threshold of 0.05. ## Your Answer. results.title: The 20% Statistician: Calculating Confidence Intervals around Standard Deviations
results.content: In this blog, I explain how to calculate confidence intervals around standard deviation estimates obtained from a sample, and show how much sample sizes in an a-priori power analysis can differ based on variation in estimates of the standard deviation.*. If we calculate a standard deviation from a sample, this value is an estimate of the true value in the population. Since the sample standard deviation is an estimate with uncertainty, we can calculate a 95% confidence interval around it. Since the estimate of the population standard deviation based on a pilot study has some uncertainty, the width of confidence intervals around the standard deviation might be a useful way to show how much variability one can expect. Use **validated or existing measures for which accurate estimates of the standard deviation in your population of interest are available**, so that you can rely on a better estimate of the standard deviation in power analyses.

results.title: Expert estimates cost of KL-Singapore HSR at S$20-25b - The Edge Malaysia
results.content: Expert estimates cost of KL-Singapore HSR at S$20-25b Expert estimates cost of KL-Singapore HSR at S$20-25b BySulhi Azman & Emir Zainul / theedgemarkets.com 05 Oct 2017, 01:57 pm KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): The cost to build the 350km high speed rail linking Kuala Lumpur and Singapore is expected to range between S$20 billion (RM60 billion) and S$25 billion, according to an estimate by Institute of Southeast Asia Studies (ISEAS). "When YTL (Corp Bhd) provided the estimate for the high speed rail in 2006, the cost that they have proposed was S$2.7 billion," ISEAS senior fellow Dr Francis E. As for the breakdown of the cost, Hutchinson said around US$3.5 billion or S$5 billion is expected to be allocated to laying of tracks, electrification and system integration, all of which is equivalent to US$10 million per kilometre. As for the civil infrastructure cost, which includes building of bridges and tunnelling works, Hutchinson said it may cost around S$15 billion. Hence, even though the Singapore portion is only 6% of the total high speed rail length, due to land scarcity, the tunnelling cost is expected to be higher," he added. "The frequency of the high speed rail service, which I understand, is about four times an hour, one being an express non-stop service, and the other three times are for shuttle servicing the in-between intermediaries stop," he added. Compared to Japan's high speed rail, Hutchinson said the frequency between an express non-stop trip between Tokyo and Osaka is about 14 times. "That is partly to amortise the expenditure, but that should also be taken into consideration in designing any high speed rail," he added, noting that "If my calculation is true, is the one-way ticket cost justified?" To recoup the investment on the high speed rail investment cost, Hutchinson noted that the railway owner must determine between collecting fare and non-fare revenue. "The Japanese, they tend to focus on the quality of their high speed rail, and the record speaks for itself," Hutchinson noted. The upcoming 350km high speed rail is a mammoth development project, which will cut the travelling time between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore to 90 minutes.

results.title: binomial distribution - How to compute confidence intervals for changes in sales, returns, and return rates in independent auction experiments? - Cross Validated
results.content:
Title: binomial distribution - How to compute confidence intervals for changes in sales, returns, and return rates in independent auction experiments? - Cross Validated
# How to compute confidence intervals for changes in sales, returns, and return rates in independent auction experiments? | **Number sold** | 500 | 600 | Random variables $ S\_A $ and $ S\_B $ |. | **Number (sold and) returned** | 200 | 300 | Random variables $ R\_A $ and $ R\_B $ |. To compute the confidence interval for the delta in the number of sales:. To compute confidence intervals for deltas in the **number of returns** and the **return rate**:. This is not an answer to most of your question, but I want to point you towards two alternative methods to determine the confidence intervals based on either the "parametric bootstrap" or the likelihood ratio approach. We can then sample a larger number of $(S\_A,S\_B,R\_A,R\_B)$ and use this to calculate the distribution of any variable of interest. If we are interested in the change in sales, one would use $\Delta S = S\_A/n\_A - S\_B/n\_B$, for the change in returns $\Delta R = R\_A/n\_A - R\_B/n\_B$, and the return rate $\Delta r = R\_A/S\_A - R\_B/S\_B$. Unfortunately, this is incorrect because it computes the % change based on the lowest observed counts (which is a random variable), as opposed to the sample size (which is a constant). In both cases the rate of returns went from 40% $(\frac{200}{500} $) to 50% ($ \frac{300}{600} )$, or again a change of 10 percentage points (not 25%). Interestingly, a previous answer by @K.Hencken, computed the differences, and CI's by bootstrapping. In the comment, the OP insisted that the relative changes is what was truly of interest, because "\*in A/B testing, relative changes are often more meaningful \*". Having said this, if the OP is absolutely set on using/presenting relative changes, and computing CI's for said relative changes, a z-test is **not** the proper approach, no matter how the variance is computed. The computations get simplified by the fact that, in the OP's case, the covariance is 0 (independence of the A and B samples). Note though that, if you use the (absolute or relative) CI's to do hypothesis tests (i.e. does the CI include 0?), you may run into cases where one is (statistically) significant, but not the other.
